title: RabbitMQ
summary: AMQP connection handshake, management API and health checks. Includes an enterprise test plan (jobs starting ent-).
description: Load tests RabbitMQ: the AMQP protocol handshake, the alarms health check, the management API overview, queue list and connection list, and a management call without credentials that must be refused. It shows how connections and the management API scale.

variables.name: host
variables.guide: The host name or IP address of the server, without a port or http://, for example redis.staging.example.com. BLASTA runs in a container, so for a service on your own machine use host.docker.internal instead of localhost.

variables.name: mgmt
variables.description: Management API URL, no trailing slash
variables.guide: The address of the management interface. Keycloak 25+: port 9000 (https://host:9000). RabbitMQ: http://host:15672. BLASTA runs in a container, so for a service on your own machine use host.docker.internal instead of localhost.

variables.name: basic
variables.description: base64(user:password) for the management API. Read from RABBITMQ_BASIC by the CLI.

jobs.name: AMQP protocol handshake
jobs.notes: Sends the AMQP 0-9-1 protocol header and checks that the broker answers with a Connection.Start frame. Every connection costs an Erlang process, so this is the connection-churn test.

jobs.name: health check: alarms
jobs.notes: Fails when a memory or disk alarm is active, i.e. when producers are being blocked.

jobs.name: overview
jobs.notes: The management dashboard's main call: global message rates and totals.

jobs.name: queue list
jobs.notes: Heavy with thousands of queues; dashboards poll it every few seconds. Add ?page=1&page_size=100 in real use.

jobs.name: connection list
jobs.notes: Every client connection with statistics. Expensive at thousands of connections.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 01 smoke
jobs.notes: Enterprise plan, step 1 of 10. One request a second for 30 seconds. Run this first, every time: it proves the address, credentials and headers are right and that the environment is up before any real load is applied. Gate: zero errors. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 02 baseline (20% load)
jobs.notes: Step 2 of 10. About a fifth of normal traffic for 5 minutes: the uncontended latency of this request. Every later result is judged against it, so record p50 and p95. Gate: at most 0.5% errors and the default latency targets. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 03 average load (SLO check)
jobs.notes: Step 3 of 10. Normal busy-hour traffic for 10 minutes. The rate is the reference job's rate: raise it to your measured production peak-hour rate. This is the run that proves (or breaks) your SLO. Gate: at most 1% errors, p95 and p99 inside the targets. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 04 peak load (2x average)
jobs.notes: Step 4 of 10. Twice the average for 10 minutes: the busiest hour of the year plus headroom. Latency may rise, but must stay in SLO; if it does not, you have no headroom. Gate: at most 2% errors, latency targets doubled. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 05 stress (ramp to 4x)
jobs.notes: Step 5 of 10. Ramps to four times average over 10 minutes, then holds for 2. Finds where it degrades and HOW: gracefully (latency rises, errors stay low) or badly (errors, timeouts, crashes, restarts). Observation only, no gate. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 06 spike (10x in 10 s)
jobs.notes: Step 6 of 10. Reaches ten times average within 10 seconds and holds for 2 minutes: a campaign email, a news link, a failover. Checks autoscaling, queue limits and load shedding. Gate: at most 5% errors, because shedding load is acceptable and crashing is not. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 07 recovery after the spike
jobs.notes: Step 7 of 10. Run IMMEDIATELY after the spike, at average load for 5 minutes. Latency and errors must return to the baseline from step 2. If they do not, something is stuck: queues, connection pools, GC, an autoscaler cool-down. Gate: same as average load. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 08 soak (1 hour at 60%)
jobs.notes: Step 8 of 10. One hour of steady load. Finds leaks and slow decay in memory, connections, file descriptors, disk, log volume and cache churn. Watch the resource graphs: any line that climbs and never flattens is a finding. Gate: at most 0.5% errors. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 09 breakpoint (find the ceiling)
jobs.notes: Step 9 of 10. Ramps to twenty times average over 20 minutes. Stop it when errors pass about 5%: the rate at that moment is your ceiling, and ceiling divided by peak is your capacity margin. Use a production-like environment, never production. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: 10 resilience window (failover / deploy)
jobs.notes: Step 10 of 10. Average load for 15 minutes. About 5 minutes in, cause the event you are testing: kill a pod or node, fail over the database, roll out a new version, drain a zone. Errors in the window are your real availability loss. Gate: at most 1% errors overall; read the time series for how long the dip lasted. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: connection storm (ramp to 10x)
jobs.notes: Ramps new connections per second to ten times normal: a fleet reconnecting after an outage, a deploy that restarts every pod, a network blip. Shows accept-queue, file descriptor and handshake limits. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

jobs.name: RabbitMQ: client reconnect storm
jobs.notes: Every producer and consumer reconnects after a broker restart. Ramps to ten times normal. Reference request: AMQP protocol handshake.

RABBITMQ_BASIC.label: RabbitMQ login (base64)
RABBITMQ_BASIC.guide: A management user with the monitoring tag. Encode it like this (macOS or Linux): `printf 'USER:PASSWORD' | base64` and paste the result.
